content.description: A black hole is not a cosmic vacuum cleaner. It is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.

hero.hook: Nothing gets out, not even light. And yet we ended up photographing its shadow.

blocks.text: For a century, black holes were only equations on paper. Then, in April 2019, astronomers showed the world a picture.

blocks.caption: Here it is: the first image of a black hole.

stops.text: Here it is: the first image of a black hole.
**The dark center.** This is the black hole's shadow. No light comes out of here. It is wider than our entire solar system.
**The glowing ring.** Gas heated to billions of degrees, whirling around the hole at close to the speed of light.
**The bottom is brighter.** That part of the gas is rushing toward us, which makes its light look stronger.
A shadow, a ring, a bright side. The rest of this course explains each of them.

blocks.text: A star spends its life in a tug of war. Gravity pulls everything inward. The heat of nuclear fusion in its core pushes outward. As long as there is fuel, the two cancel out.
When a very heavy star, at least 20 times the mass of the Sun, runs out of fuel, the push stops. The core caves in within seconds, and the outer layers are blown away in a **supernova**.

blocks.caption: This is the Crab Nebula: the wreck of a star that Chinese astronomers watched explode in the year 1054.

stops.text: This is the Crab Nebula: the wreck of a star that Chinese astronomers watched explode in the year 1054.
**The glowing shreds** are the star's outer layers. Almost a thousand years later, they are still flying outward at about 1,500 km per second.
**At the center, the crushed core.** Here it became a neutron star: a ball about 20 km wide, heavier than the Sun.
Had the star been heavier, nothing could have stopped the collapse. The core would have become a black hole.

blocks.text: In that case, theory says the matter is crushed into a [[singularity]]. Around it lies the [[event horizon]]: an invisible border. Cross it, and there is no way back.
If you fell feet first toward a small black hole, gravity would pull far harder on your feet than on your head. Physicists have a serious name for what happens next: “spaghettification.”

blocks.explanation: It is not a surface you could stand on. It is a point of no return: inside it, even light cannot escape.
options: A solid surface, like the crust of a planet.
The bright ring of gas we see in the picture.
The border past which nothing can come back.

sections.title: A star that loses its fight

blocks.explanation: Earth would keep circling exactly as before. A black hole's pull depends on its mass and on distance, like any other object. We would just freeze in the dark.
options: True
False
blocks.prompt: If the Sun were swapped for a black hole of the **same mass**, Earth would be sucked in.

blocks.text: Black holes only swallow what comes very close. Some, though, are giants. At the heart of almost every galaxy sits a **supermassive** black hole, millions or billions of times heavier than the Sun.

blocks.caption: This is the galaxy M87, seen by the Hubble Space Telescope. Two things stand out.

stops.text: This is the galaxy M87, seen by the Hubble Space Telescope. Two things stand out.
**The bright core.** Hidden inside is a black hole 6.5 billion times heavier than the Sun. It is the one in the famous picture.
**The blue streak** is a jet of matter 5,000 light-years long, fired out at nearly the speed of light.
The black hole itself stays invisible. What gives it away is everything around it.

blocks.text: Gas falling toward a black hole does not drop straight in. It spirals, forming an [[accretion disk]]. Friction heats it until it shines. So to photograph something black, you photograph its glowing surroundings.
There is a catch. Seen from Earth, the black hole of M87 looks as small as an orange on the Moon. To see a detail that fine, you would need a telescope as wide as the planet.

steps.text: Nobody can build that. So in **April 2017**, astronomers try a trick: link telescopes that are thousands of kilometers apart.
**Chile.** At 5,000 m in the Atacama desert, two observatories, including ALMA and its 66 dishes.
**Hawaii, Arizona, Mexico.** Each site records the same patch of sky at the same instant, timed by atomic clocks.
**Spain**, on a peak of the Sierra Nevada.

Add a station at the South Pole, off this map, and you get eight telescopes on six sites. Combined by [[interferometry]], they act like a single dish almost as wide as Earth: the Event Horizon Telescope.

blocks.text: Nobody can build that. So in April 2017, astronomers try a trick: link telescopes that are thousands of kilometers apart. Chile. At 5,000 m in the Atacama desert, two observatories, including ALMA and its 66 dishes. Hawaii, Arizona, Mexico. Each site records the same patch of sky at the same instant, timed by atomic clocks. Spain, on a peak of the Sierra Nevada. Add a station at the South Pole, off this map, and you get eight telescopes on six sites. Combined by interferometry, they act like a single dish almost as wide as Earth: the Event Horizon Telescope.

blocks.caption: This is what one of those sites looks like: ALMA, in Chile, at night.

stops.text: This is what one of those sites looks like: ALMA, in Chile, at night.
**One dish.** It is 12 m wide and does not collect visible light. It listens to radio waves, which pass through the dust that hides the black hole.
**And many more.** Working together, the dishes of one site already act as one big telescope. The same trick is then repeated across the whole planet.

blocks.text: The observation produced about 5 petabytes of data: too much to send over the internet. Half a ton of hard drives was flown to the labs by plane. The drives from the South Pole had to wait months for the polar winter to end.

blocks.explanation: The telescopes recorded radio waves, which our eyes cannot see. Orange was chosen to show brightness: the brighter the signal, the lighter the color.
options: True
False
blocks.prompt: The orange color in the picture is the **real color** of the black hole's ring.

sections.title: A telescope the size of Earth

blocks.text: Four nights of observation, then two years of computing by more than 200 researchers. The result matches what Albert Einstein's theory of gravity, published in **1915**, predicted for the shape and size of the shadow.

blocks.caption: Albert Einstein in 1921. He doubted that black holes could really exist. His own equations said otherwise.

blocks.explanation: Nothing escapes from inside. The ring is gas outside the event horizon, heated until it glows, with its light bent around the hole by gravity.
options: Hot gas circling just outside the black hole.
The surface of the black hole itself.
Light escaping from inside the black hole.
blocks.prompt: In the picture, what is the **orange ring** made of?

blocks.text: In **2022**, the same team released a second picture. This time, the target was much closer to home: Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the center of our own galaxy, the Milky Way.

blocks.caption: Sagittarius A, 27,000 light-years away. It looks a lot like the first one.

stops.text: Sagittarius A*, 27,000 light-years away. It looks a lot like the first one.
**The same dark shadow.** This black hole is about 1,600 times lighter than the one in M87, but 2,000 times closer. In our sky, the two rings look almost the same size.
**Three bright knots.** The gas here circles the hole in minutes, so the picture kept changing while it was being taken. These spots are partly an effect of that blur.

blocks.text: In **1974**, the British physicist Stephen Hawking showed that black holes should not be completely black. Because of quantum effects at the horizon, they should give off a very faint glow: [[Hawking radiation]].
A black hole left alone would therefore slowly lose mass and, in the end, evaporate. For a real one, that would take unimaginably longer than the current age of the universe.
There is now a second way to detect them. Since **2015**, detectors have picked up gravitational waves: tiny ripples in space sent out when two black holes collide.

blocks.explanation: From a prediction on paper to a photograph: just over a hundred years.
items: Einstein publishes his theory of gravity
Hawking predicts that black holes glow faintly
First picture of a black hole, in M87
Picture of the black hole at the center of the Milky Way
blocks.prompt: Last question. Put a century of black hole science **in order**.

blocks.text:
A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape past the event horizon.
We cannot see the hole itself. We see the hot gas around it and the shadow it casts.
The first picture, in 2019, needed eight telescopes working as one, as wide as Earth.

Accretion disk.explanation: Structure of gas and dust rotating around a massive object (such as a black hole), heated by friction and shining intensely.

Event horizon.explanation: "Boundary" of a black hole beyond which nothing can return, not even light. It is not a physical surface but a mathematical limit: the speed required to escape exceeds that of light.

Hawking radiation.explanation: A very faint glow that a black hole should give off because of quantum effects at its edge, predicted by Stephen Hawking in 1974.

Interferometry.explanation: Technique consisting of combining signals from several distant telescopes to obtain a resolution equivalent to that of a giant telescope.

The event horizon.explanation: The "boundary" of a black hole beyond which nothing can return, not even light. It is not a physical surface but a mathematical limit: the speed required to escape exceeds that of light.

The gravitational singularity.explanation: Point at the center of a black hole where density theoretically becomes infinite. The equations of known physics cease to function there - a quantum theory of gravity (not yet developed) would be necessary to describe what happens there.

accretion disk.explanation: A ring of gas and dust spinning around a black hole at huge speed. Friction heats it until it glows.

event horizon.explanation: The boundary around a black hole. Anything that crosses it, light included, can never come back out.

gravitational singularity.explanation: Point at the center of a black hole where density theoretically becomes infinite. The equations of known physics cease to function there - a quantum theory of gravity (not yet developed) would be necessary to describe what happens there.

interferometry.explanation: A technique that combines the signals of several distant telescopes so that they act like one giant telescope.

singularity.explanation: The center of a black hole according to theory: a point where matter is crushed to extreme density and our equations stop working.
